> [!info] TL;DR
> Vaswani et al. (2017) threw out the RNN entirely. They built a sequence model using only attention and feed-forward layers, with **multi-head self-attention** at its core. The result was the **Transformer** — the architecture behind GPT, BERT, T5, Llama, Claude, Gemini, and essentially every modern LLM. This is arguably the most influential neural architecture paper of the 2017–2025 era.

excerpt: The authors asked a provocative question: **what if attention itself is enough?** RNNs serve two purposes — they mix information across positions, and they introduce nonlinearity. Attention can do the first (and do it with arbitrary-length dependencies in O(1) path length), and feed-forward layers can do the second. Removing the recurrence gives full parallelism on GPUs.

excerpt:
- **Quadratic attention cost**: `O(n²)` memory and compute for sequence length `n`. The paper's experiments used ~50-token sentences, so this was not a problem; it became the central obstacle at long context. See [[12 - Sparse Attention]], [[13 - Linear Attention]], [[11 - FlashAttention]].
- **Post-norm instability**: training the original Transformer required careful warmup. Pre-norm ([[02 - Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm|pre-norm]]) made training much more stable and became the default.
- **Sinusoidal PE is weak**: it works but learned positional embeddings and especially [[08 - RoPE|RoPE]] gave better length generalization.
- **Encoder-decoder is overkill for many tasks**: GPT-2 would show that decoder-only is often sufficient and simpler.
- **No MoE**: every token goes through every parameter. [[15 - Mixture of Experts Transformer|MoE]] later added conditional computation for much larger effective model sizes.

> [!info] TL;DR
> BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) showed that pretraining a Transformer encoder with two simple unsupervised objectives — Masked Language Modeling (MLM) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) — produces representations that transfer to almost any NLP classification or QA task with minimal fine-tuning. BERT established the **pretrain-then-finetune** paradigm that still dominates NLP.
Devlin, J., Chang, M.-W., Lee, K., & Toutanova, K. (2019). *BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding*. NAACL 2019. arXiv:1810.04805.

In 2017, the standard recipe for NLP transfer learning was: pretrain word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) → use them as input features to a task-specific architecture (CNN, BiLSTM, etc.). This worked but was shallow — the pretrained representations captured only static word meaning, not syntax, semantics, or context.

[[02 - Vaswani Attention Is All You Need 2017|Vaswani 2017]] and GPT-1 (Radford 2018) had shown that you could pretrain a Transformer end-to-end and then fine-tune. But GPT-1 used a **decoder-only** architecture with left-to-right (causal) language modeling, which meant the representation of each token could only see its left context. For tasks like NER, sentiment, or QA — which benefit from bidirectional context — this was a real limitation.

BERT's contribution was to ask: what if we pretrain a *bidirectional* encoder that can see both left and right context for every token? The challenge is that standard language modeling is left-to-right; you cannot predict the next token if you have already seen it. BERT solved this with **masked language modeling** — randomly mask some tokens and predict them from the surrounding context on both sides.
BERT is a multi-layer [[07 - BERT|Transformer encoder]]. The paper released two sizes:
BERT Base was deliberately sized to match GPT-1's parameter count to enable head-to-head comparison.
The input is a sequence of WordPiece tokens (see [[03 - WordPiece]]). Each token's representation is the sum of:

1. **Token embedding** — learned lookup.
2. **Segment embedding** — learned "sentence A" vs "sentence B" indicator (for NSP).
3. **Position embedding** — learned, absolute position up to 512.

Special tokens: `[CLS]` (always the first token; its final hidden state is used as the aggregate sequence representation for classification), `[SEP]` (sentence boundary), `[MASK]` (placeholder for MLM), `[PAD]`.
Randomly mask 15% of WordPiece tokens. Of those:

- 80% replaced with `[MASK]`.
- 10% replaced with a random token.
- 10% left unchanged.

The model predicts the original token at each masked position. The 80/10/10 split is a mismatch-distribution trick: pure `[MASK]` never appears at fine-tune time, so the small random-replacement and unchanged fractions force the model to maintain useful representations for every token, not just `[MASK]`.

Only masked positions contribute to the loss — this makes MLM less sample-efficient than causal LM (which has a loss on every token), but the bidirectional context more than compensates in downstream quality.

For tasks like QA or NLI that involve sentence-pair reasoning, BERT adds an auxiliary binary classification: given two sentences A and B, is B the actual next sentence in the source corpus, or a random sentence?

50% of training pairs are real consecutive sentences; 50% have B sampled randomly. The `[CLS]` token's representation is fed to a binary classifier. Later work (RoBERTa) showed NSP adds little value; it was dropped in most subsequent encoder pretraining.

- BooksCorpus (800M words)
- English Wikipedia (2,500M words)
Total ~3.3B words. Pretraining took 4 days on 64 TPU v2 chips for BERT Large — nontrivial but accessible by 2018 standards.

For downstream tasks, BERT is fine-tuned by replacing the output head with a task-specific layer and training end-to-end on the downstream dataset for a few epochs. The paper showed four canonical task setups:

- **Single-sentence classification** (SST-2 sentiment, etc.): `[CLS]` hidden state → linear classifier.
- **Sentence-pair classification** (MNLI, QQP, etc.): same as above, with both sentences concatenated.
- **Question answering** (SQuAD): for each token, predict start and end probabilities of the answer span.
- **Sequence labeling** (NER): per-token classifier.
Fine-tuning is cheap: SQuAD took ~30 minutes on a single TPU.
BERT set new state of the art on 11 NLP tasks:
The improvements were not marginal; BERT moved the field decisively. Within months, virtually every NLP benchmark had a BERT-based leader.

Every token's representation aggregates information from both left and right neighbors. For tasks like NER or QA, where the surrounding context is essential, this is materially better than a left-to-right decoder.

The paper made the recipe explicit: pretrain on cheap unlabeled text → fine-tune on small labeled data. This worked so well that within a year it was the *default* approach for any NLP task with limited labels.

Because BERT's representations were already strong, fine-tuning required only a few epochs on a small dataset. This brought transfer learning within reach of any research lab, not just large companies.
Using a single token's representation as the input to a task head is simple and effective. The convention persists across most encoder and encoder-decoder models today.

excerpt:
- **NSP was a wash**. RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) removed NSP, used more data, larger batches, and dynamic masking — strictly better. The lesson: BERT's *architecture* was right; its *pretraining recipe* was conservative.
- **Static maximum length of 512**. BERT cannot natively process long documents. Longformer, BigBird, and other long-context encoders addressed this with sparse attention.
- **WordPiece + cased/uncased vocabulary** is brittle for non-English text and code. SentencePiece and BPE-based tokenizers became standard.
- **Encoder-only is awkward for generation**. BERT cannot be used directly as a language model. GPT-style decoder-only models eventually dominated because they handle both understanding and generation with a single architecture.
- **Whole-word masking helps**. Later Chinese and multilingual BERT variants adopted whole-word masking to avoid the model "cheating" by predicting only sub-tokens.

- **RoBERTa** (Facebook, 2019): optimized pretraining recipe; same architecture, better results.
- **ALBERT** (Google, 2019): parameter sharing across layers; smaller, faster.
- **DistilBERT** (HuggingFace, 2019): 6-layer distillation of BERT; ~60% smaller, ~60% faster, retains 95%+ quality.
- **DeBERTa** (Microsoft, 2020): disentangled attention; better position/word representation separation.
- **ELECTRA** (Stanford/Google, 2020): replaced-token detection pretraining, far more sample-efficient.
- **Sentence-BERT** (2019): siamese fine-tune for sentence embeddings.
BERT reshaped NLP in three concrete ways:

1. **Established pretrain-finetune as universal**. After BERT, no serious NLP system trained from scratch — every model was either pretrained or distilled from a pretrained model.
2. **Made Transformers the default encoder**. CNNs and BiLSTMs essentially disappeared from new NLP architectures after 2019.
3. **Created the open-weights ecosystem**. BERT was released on day one (on arXiv and Google's repo) and quickly appeared in HuggingFace's model hub. This set the precedent for the open-weights culture that defined the 2018–2025 LLM era.

For inference and production deployments, BERT remains a workhorse in 2024–2026: search ranking, intent classification, moderation, embedding generation. The model that pioneered the recipe is also the model that still runs in production at scale.

> [!info] TL;DR
> T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer) reframed every NLP task as **text-in, text-out** — translation, classification, QA, summarization, and even regression all become seq2seq problems with task-specific text prefixes. The paper ran a massive systematic study of pretraining objectives, datasets, and architectures, then trained a single model on the resulting recipe. T5 set the standard for encoder-decoder LLMs and pioneered the "task prefix" convention that survives in modern instruction-tuned models.

Raffel, C., Shazeer, N., Roberts, A., Lee, K., Narang, S., Matena, M., Zhou, Y., Li, W., & Liu, P. (2020). *Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer*. JMLR 21(140). arXiv:1910.10683.

By 2019, transfer learning in NLP was fragmented. BERT (encoder-only) excelled at understanding tasks but could not generate. GPT-2 (decoder-only) could generate but was awkward for classification. Encoder-decoder models like BART existed but were not systematically studied. Worse, every task had a different "head" — a classifier for sentiment, a span predictor for QA, a sequence generator for translation — making it hard to do multi-task training or zero-shot transfer.

T5 asked: what if we **frame every task as text-to-text**? Then we only need one model, one loss, one training loop, and one inference API. Translation: `translate English to German: <input>` → `<output>`. Sentiment: `sentiment: <input>` → `positive` or `negative`. QA: `question: <q> context: <c>` → `<answer>`. Summarization: `summarize: <input>` → `<summary>`.

This unification has far-reaching implications. It removes the need for task-specific heads, lets a single model handle arbitrary tasks, and — critically — lets you mix tasks in training simply by including the task prefix.
T5 uses the original Vaswani encoder-decoder architecture with a few modifications:

Instead of post-norm (`LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x))`), T5 uses pre-norm (`x + Sublayer(LayerNorm(x))`). This was an early adoption of a change that would become standard for training stability. See [[02 - Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm]].

Instead of sinusoidal or learned absolute positional embeddings, T5 uses a **relative position bias** added to the attention scores. For each attention head, a learned scalar `b_{i-j}` is added to the attention logit between query position `i` and key position `j`. Positions beyond a cutoff (~128) share buckets, so the model has a smooth notion of relative position that extrapolates beyond training lengths.
This was an important step toward [[08 - RoPE|RoPE]]-style relative encodings, which would become the modern default.
T5 uses `gelu_new` (a GELU variant) in the feed-forward layer, not the SwiGLU that later became standard.
The 11B model used a sparse feed-forward layer (only certain experts active) to keep compute manageable — an early hint at [[15 - Mixture of Experts Transformer|MoE]].
The paper systematically compared many pretraining objectives:

- Causal LM (GPT-style)
- Masked LM (BERT-style)
- Prefix LM (a hybrid)
- Span corruption (BART-style)
- Replace-corrupted spans with sentinel tokens

The winner was **span corruption**: mask contiguous spans of tokens, replace each with a single unique sentinel token (`<extra_id_0>`, `<extra_id_1>`, ...), and train the decoder to output the masked spans separated by sentinels.
Example:

```
Input:  The quick <X> jumps over <Y> dog
Target: <X> brown fox <Y> the lazy
```
This objective has several nice properties:

- **Bidirectional** encoder (sees both sides of each span).
- **Generative** decoder (must produce text).
- **Variable span lengths** (sampled from a geometric distribution) teach the model to handle multi-token reconstruction.
- **Sentinel tokens** make it unambiguous which span goes where.
The final recipe: mask 15% of tokens, with mean span length 3.
The authors built a new pretraining corpus, **C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus)**:

- ~750GB of cleaned English text from Common Crawl (April 2019).
- Filters: remove non-English, remove boilerplate (menus, code), deduplicate line-by-line, remove documents with bad punctuation/length patterns.
- ~156B tokens after filtering.
C4 became a standard pretraining dataset for years, used by T5, LaMDA, and many subsequent models.

The paper's most ambitious experiment was a **mixture-of-tasks** pretraining: mix span corruption with downstream tasks (translation, QA, summarization) directly in pretraining. Each example has a task prefix, and the model sees a stream of mixed-task examples.
The result: a single model that can perform all the mixed-in tasks at zero-shot inference, just by using the appropriate task prefix. This was a precursor to modern instruction-tuned LLMs.

T5 achieved SOTA on GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, and CNN/DailyMail summarization at release time. The 11B model reached 89.3 on SuperGLUE, exceeding the previous SOTA by ~4 points and approaching human-level performance (which is ~89.8 on SuperGLUE).

The smaller variants also performed well, making T5 a popular choice for fine-tuning on task-specific data — especially for seq2seq tasks (summarization, translation) where decoder-only models are awkward.

Framing every task as text generation is a powerful abstraction. It removes architectural differences between tasks, enables multi-task training trivially, and provides a uniform API. The convention was inherited by all modern instruction-tuned LLMs — even decoder-only models like Llama-3 use task prefixes.

BART had introduced denoising seq2seq, but T5's systematic comparison showed span corruption with sentinels was the best variant. It gave the encoder bidirectional context *and* trained a generative decoder — useful for both understanding and generation.
heading_path: Span Corruption as a Generative-Yet-Bidirectional Objective

excerpt: This was an important architectural improvement over absolute positional embeddings. It gave T5 modest length extrapolation (could handle longer inputs than it saw in training) and set the stage for RoPE.

C4's careful filtering removed a lot of the noise that hurt earlier Common Crawl-based models. The paper showed that *data quality* mattered as much as *data quantity* — a finding that [[11 - Training/Pretraining/01 - Pretraining Objectives and Scaling Laws|Chinchilla]] later reinforced.

- **Encoder-decoder is parameter-inefficient**. For a given parameter budget, decoder-only models generally match or beat encoder-decoder on most tasks. By 2022, the field largely converged on decoder-only.
- **Span corruption is not natural language**. Sentinels never appear at inference time, creating a train/test mismatch. Modern instruction tuning replaced span corruption entirely.
- **No instruction tuning**. T5's prefix mechanism was the closest thing to instruction tuning at the time, but it lacked the conversational alignment that [[07 - InstructGPT 2022]] (and subsequent production chat assistants like ChatGPT, late 2022) would later establish.
- **2048-token context**. Same limit as GPT-3. Modern long-context models reach 100k–1M tokens.

- **T5-v1.1**: improved pretraining recipe, released by Google.
- **mT5**: multilingual T5 pretrained on 101 languages.
- **Flan-T5** (2022): instruction-tuned T5 — performed much better on zero-shot tasks. See [[12 - Fine-Tuning/Instruction Tuning/03 - Instruction Tuning and Chat Templates]].
- **CodeT5**: variant for code understanding/generation.
- **UL2** (2022): generalized span corruption to a mixture of denoising objectives.
T5's contributions outlasted the model itself:

1. **Text-to-text framing as default**. Every instruction-tuned LLM in 2024+ is essentially a text-to-text model. The task prefix survives in prompts like `Translate to French: ...` or `Summarize: ...`.
2. **Encoder-decoder as a viable LLM architecture**. While decoder-only dominates, encoder-decoder is still used for translation (MarianMT, NLLB) and dense retrieval (T5-based encoders).
3. **C4 as a benchmark pretraining corpus**. Used by hundreds of subsequent papers as a controlled pretraining dataset.
4. **Systematic study of pretraining choices**. The paper's ablations on objectives, datasets, and architectures set a precedent: large-scale systematic studies are valuable, not just headline SOTA results.

For practitioners in 2024–2026, Flan-T5 is still a popular open-weights model for seq2seq tasks where decoder-only models are overkill — summarization, translation, classification with structured outputs.

> [!info] TL;DR
> GPT-1 demonstrated that pretraining a decoder-only Transformer on unlabeled text with a causal language modeling objective, followed by minimal task-specific fine-tuning, achieves strong performance across diverse NLP tasks (classification, entailment, similarity, multiple choice). GPT-1 established the **pretrain-then-finetune** recipe for generative models, complementing BERT's encoder approach, and laid the architectural foundation for the entire GPT family.
Radford, A., Narasimhan, K., Salimans, T., & Sutskever, I. (2018). *Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training*. OpenAI technical report (unpublished; circulated as a PDF).

By 2018, NLP faced a data problem. Supervised learning required labeled datasets for every task — and most tasks had limited labeled data (a few thousand examples). Unsupervised pretraining had been explored for word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) and for ELMo (which used bidirectional language model features), but no one had shown that a single pretrained Transformer could be fine-tuned to excel across many tasks with minimal task-specific architecture.

The key insight: generative pretraining (predicting the next token) on a large unlabeled corpus teaches the model syntax, semantics, world knowledge, and reasoning patterns. Then, a small amount of supervised fine-tuning adapts the model to specific tasks. This recipe — "generative pretraining + discriminative fine-tuning" — is the "G" and "P" in GPT.

The paper's contribution was not a new architecture (the Transformer was already a year old) but a demonstration that the pretrain-finetune recipe, applied to a decoder-only Transformer, worked across many tasks with minimal modification.
GPT-1 is a 12-layer decoder-only Transformer:

| Property            | Value           |
|---------------------|-----------------|
| Parameters          | 117M            |
| Layers              | 12              |
| Hidden dimension    | 768             |
| Attention heads     | 12              |
| Context window      | 512 tokens      |
| Vocabulary          | ~40K BPE        |
| Positional encoding | Learned         |
| Activation          | GELU            |
The architecture is the standard Transformer decoder from [[02 - Vaswani Attention Is All You Need 2017|Vaswani 2017]], with causal masking (each token can only attend to itself and previous tokens).
Train on a large unlabeled corpus using the causal language modeling objective:
where `u_i` is the i-th token and `k` is the context window size.

**Training data**: BooksCorpus (~7,000 unique unpublished books, ~800M words). The choice of long-form continuous text (books, not web snippets) was important — it taught the model long-range dependencies and discourse structure.
**Training setup**: 1 month on 8 GPUs (P6000). The model learned to predict the next token with reasonable perplexity, demonstrating that the unsupervised objective provided useful signal.
For each downstream task, take the pretrained model and add a small task-specific head (usually a linear layer). Fine-tune end-to-end on the labeled dataset.
The key innovation: **input transformations, not architecture changes**. GPT-1 handles diverse tasks by formatting the input differently, not by changing the model:

- **Classification** (e.g., sentiment): `[START] text [EXTRACT]` → linear head.
- **Entailment** (e.g., SNLI): `[START] premise [DELIM] hypothesis [EXTRACT]` → linear head.
- **Similarity** (e.g., STS): `[START] text1 [DELIM] text2 [EXTRACT]` and `[START] text2 [DELIM] text1 [EXTRACT]` (both orderings, sum) → linear head.
- **Multiple choice** (e.g., RACE): `[START] context question [DELIM] answer [EXTRACT]` per option → softmax over options.

This **unified input format** meant the same pretrained model could be fine-tuned for any task with minimal architectural modification — just a linear output head. This was a significant departure from task-specific architectures (CNNs for classification, attention networks for entailment, siamese networks for similarity).
GPT-1 achieved state-of-the-art or near-SOTA on 9 of 12 tasks evaluated:

The most striking result was on RACE (reading comprehension): GPT-1 jumped 7.5 points, suggesting that pretraining on books gave the model genuine reading comprehension ability. The SST-2 regression showed that for very simple tasks (binary sentiment), task-specific architectures could still win — but only barely.

BooksCorpus provided continuous, coherent long-form text. This taught the model discourse-level patterns (narrative structure, character tracking, argument flow) that short-text corpora (Wikipedia, news) could not. The choice of pretraining data was as important as the architecture.

Causal language modeling is universal — every text sequence is a valid training example. There's no need for special masking (BERT's MLM) or paired data (translation). This makes it trivial to scale pretraining to arbitrary corpora, which would prove crucial as GPT-2 and GPT-3 scaled up.

By formatting inputs rather than redesigning the model, GPT-1 demonstrated that a single pretrained Transformer could handle diverse tasks. This unified the field — instead of building a different architecture per task, researchers could focus on pretraining and fine-tuning.

The decoder-only architecture is simpler than encoder-decoder (no cross-attention) and supports generation natively. While BERT (released 6 months later) would show that bidirectional encoders are better for understanding tasks, GPT-1's decoder-only choice proved prescient — it's the architecture of all modern LLMs (GPT-3/4, Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek).

- **Small by modern standards**: 117M parameters is tiny. GPT-2 (1.5B) and GPT-3 (175B) would show what scale could unlock.
- **Short context**: 512 tokens. Modern LLMs handle 100K–1M tokens.
- **No alignment**: GPT-1 produced raw text completions, not helpful responses. It would take InstructGPT (2022) to add the alignment layer that made GPT-class models useful as assistants.
- **Limited evaluation**: the paper evaluated on standard NLP benchmarks, not on the generative tasks (writing, coding, reasoning) that would later define LLM evaluation.
GPT-1's contributions were conceptual and methodological, not architectural:
1. **Established the GPT recipe**: pretrain (causal LM) → fine-tune (task-specific head). Every subsequent GPT model follows this recipe, with RLHF added for alignment starting at InstructGPT.

2. **Validated decoder-only Transformers for NLP**: before GPT-1, the field was uncertain whether encoder (BERT-style) or decoder (GPT-style) would dominate. GPT-1 showed that decoders work; GPT-2 and GPT-3 would show they scale better.

3. **Unified input formatting**: the idea of formatting inputs to handle diverse tasks (rather than redesigning models) anticipated the text-to-text framing of T5 and the instruction tuning of modern LLMs.

4. **Pretrained models as a product**: GPT-1 was OpenAI's first major public model release. It established the pattern (release pretrained model, let researchers fine-tune) that would define the open-source LLM ecosystem.

For AI engineers, GPT-1 is mostly of historical interest — modern LLMs are 1000× larger and far more capable. But understanding GPT-1 clarifies *why* the field converged on decoder-only Transformers and pretrain-finetune: these choices were not inevitable, but the empirical evidence (starting with GPT-1) made them the default.

excerpt: GPT-1's input formatting was a quiet but profound innovation. Instead of redesigning the model for each task, GPT-1 formats the input differently:

```
Classification:  [START] text [EXTRACT] → linear head → class
Entailment:      [START] premise [DELIM] hypothesis [EXTRACT] → linear head → entail/neutral/contradict
Similarity:      [START] text1 [DELIM] text2 [EXTRACT] + [START] text2 [DELIM] text1 [EXTRACT] → sum → linear head → score
Multiple choice: [START] context question [DELIM] answer_i [EXTRACT] per option → softmax over options
```
The `[START]`, `[DELIM]`, `[EXTRACT]` tokens delimit input structure for the model. The same pretrained Transformer processes all formats; only the linear head differs.
**Why this mattered**:

1. **Unified architecture**: one model, one architecture, all tasks. No more CNN-for-classification, siamese-for-similarity, etc.
2. **Pretraining transfers**: the pretrained model's understanding of language transfers to all tasks via the same backbone.
3. **Anticipated instruction tuning**: the format-driven approach prefigured T5's text-to-text framing (2019) and modern instruction tuning (FLAN, InstructGPT, 2022+). The idea that "the input format tells the model what to do" is the foundation of modern LLM prompting.
GPT-1 was pretrained on BooksCorpus (~7,000 unpublished books, ~800M words). The choice was deliberate:
**Why BooksCorpus, not Wikipedia or CommonCrawl?**

- **Long-form continuous text**: books are coherent narratives, teaching long-range dependencies (character tracking, plot, argument flow).
- **Discourse structure**: books have chapters, scenes, arguments — teaching the model how language is structured at the document level.
- **No web noise**: CommonCrawl (used by later models) has machine-generated text, SEO spam, and boilerplate. BooksCorpus is curated (even if "unpublished").

**Why this was important**: a model pretrained on short snippets (Wikipedia articles) learns word-level and sentence-level patterns but not discourse. A model pretrained on books learns that text has long-range structure — character A mentioned in chapter 1 reappears in chapter 5; an argument set up in paragraph 1 is resolved in paragraph 10.

**Limitations**: BooksCorpus is small by modern standards (800M words vs. GPT-3's 500B tokens). GPT-1 was therefore limited in the world knowledge it could acquire. Later models (GPT-2, GPT-3) used much larger and more diverse corpora (WebText, CommonCrawl filtered).
GPT-1's 117M parameters seem tiny by modern standards, but the choice was constrained:

- **Compute budget**: 8 P6000 GPUs for 1 month. Modern 70B models need 1000s of H100s for months.
- **BooksCorpus size**: with 800M words and 117M params, the model was near compute-optimal (Chinchilla would later suggest ~16B tokens for 117M params; BooksCorpus has ~1B tokens, so GPT-1 was undertrained by modern standards).
- **Memory**: 117M fits in 1 GPU for training; larger models would need model parallelism (immature in 2018).

The undertraining explains why GPT-1 wasn't yet impressive on generation — it could write coherent sentences but not sustained paragraphs. GPT-2 (1.5B params, 10× more data) was the first GPT model that could generate convincing long-form text.

1. **Too small**: 117M was insufficient. GPT-2 (1.5B) showed what 13× more parameters unlocked.
2. **Too little data**: 800M words was 1000× less than Chinchilla-optimal. Modern small models (Llama 3 8B) train on 15T tokens.
3. **No alignment**: GPT-1 produced raw text completions, not helpful responses. It would take InstructGPT (2022) to add RLHF alignment.
4. **No in-context learning**: GPT-1 didn't demonstrate ICL — that emerged at GPT-3 scale (175B).
5. **Task-specific heads**: GPT-1 used linear heads for each task. Modern LLMs use the model itself (via prompting) for all tasks — no task-specific architecture.
These "mistakes" are unfair in hindsight — GPT-1 established the recipe that subsequent models scaled. But they show how far the field has come.

> [!info] TL;DR
> ViT applied the standard Transformer encoder (with no convolutional components) to images by splitting them into 16×16 patches, embedding each patch, and processing the sequence with self-attention. With enough pretraining data (JFT-300M, 300M images), ViT matched or exceeded CNN-based SOTA on ImageNet while using fewer parameters and compute. ViT proved that Transformers are domain-agnostic sequence models — the same architecture that works for text works for images, audio, and other modalities.

Dosovitskiy, A., Beyer, L., Kolesnikov, A., Weissenborn, D., Zhai, X., Unterthiner, T., Dehghani, M., Minderer, M., Heigold, G., Gelly, S., Uszkoreit, J., & Houlsby, N. (2021). *An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale*. ICLR 2021. arXiv:2010.11929.

By 2020, Transformers dominated NLP (BERT, GPT-2, T5) but CNNs still dominated computer vision. The inductive biases of CNNs — locality (each filter sees only a small region), translation invariance (filters are shared across the image), and hierarchy (early layers detect edges, later layers detect objects) — seemed essential for vision.

Attempts to apply Transformers to images had been limited by the O(N²) cost of attention. A 224×224 image has 50,176 pixels; full attention over pixels would be 2.5B operations per layer — impractical. Prior work (Stand-Alone Self-Attention, Local Relation Networks) used local attention windows, but this reintroduced the locality bias and didn't clearly beat CNNs.

ViT's key insight: don't apply attention to pixels. Apply it to *patches*. Split the image into 16×16 patches (224×224 → 14×14 = 196 patches), embed each patch, and process the resulting 196-token sequence with a standard Transformer. This makes the sequence length manageable (196 vs 50,176) and lets you use the exact same Transformer architecture that works for NLP.
ViT is a standard Transformer encoder (from [[02 - Vaswani Attention Is All You Need 2017|Vaswani 2017]]), with image-specific input processing:

1. Split the 224×224×3 image into 16×16 patches → 14×14 = 196 patches.
2. Flatten each patch to a 768-dimensional vector (16×16×3 = 768).
3. Project with a linear layer to the model dimension (typically 768).
This is equivalent to a convolution with 16×16 kernel, stride 16, and 768 output channels — but conceptually simpler.
Prepend a learnable `[CLS]` token to the patch sequence. The `[CLS]` token's final hidden state is used as the image representation for classification. This is borrowed directly from BERT.
Add learned absolute positional embeddings to the patch embeddings. The model needs to know which patch came from where in the image, since attention is permutation-invariant.
A standard Transformer encoder: `L` layers of multi-head self-attention + feed-forward, with pre-norm and residual connections. No vision-specific components — the same architecture as BERT.
The `[CLS]` token's final hidden state → linear layer → class logits. During pretraining, this head is replaced by an MLP; during fine-tuning, it's a linear classifier.

  Split --> Patches[196 patches, each 16×16×3=768]
  Patches --> Linear[Linear projection to d_model]

  Final --> CLSOut[[CLS] output: 768]
  CLSOut --> Head[Linear classification head]
  Head --> Logits[Class logits]
```
ViT's success depended critically on pretraining data scale. The paper compared three datasets:

| Dataset          | Size         | Result                                     |
|------------------|--------------|--------------------------------------------|
| ImageNet-1K      | 1.3M images  | ViT underperforms ResNet — insufficient data|
| ImageNet-21K     | 14M images   | ViT matches ResNet                          |
| JFT-300M         | 300M images  | ViT exceeds ResNet, fewer params + compute  |

The key finding: **ViT lacks the inductive biases of CNNs** (locality, translation invariance). CNNs can learn from small datasets because their architecture encodes useful priors. ViT must *learn* these priors from data, which requires large-scale pretraining.

With JFT-300M (300M images), ViT learns the priors and exceeds CNNs. With ImageNet-1K (1.3M images), ViT cannot learn the priors and underperforms. This "data hunger" was the main criticism of ViT and motivated subsequent work (DeiT, SWAG, DINOv2) that made ViT competitive with less data.
ViT matched or exceeded CNN-based SOTA on ImageNet, with fewer parameters and less pretraining compute:

The most important comparison was on compute efficiency: ViT-Large achieved 85.2% with ~2,500 TPU-days of pretraining, while Noisy Student (a CNN-based approach) achieved 88.4% with ~9,000 TPU-days. ViT was more compute-efficient at scale.

By splitting the image into 16×16 patches, ViT reduces the sequence length from 50,176 to 196 — manageable for standard attention. The patch size is a trade-off: smaller patches give finer detail but longer sequences; larger patches are coarser but faster. 16×16 is a common default.

ViT uses the exact same Transformer encoder as BERT — no vision-specific components. This means all the NLP research on Transformer optimization (FlashAttention, better positional encodings, scaling laws) transfers directly to vision. This cross-domain transfer has been hugely valuable.

CNNs encode useful priors (locality, translation invariance) in their architecture. ViT learns these priors from data. With enough data, learned priors are *better* than hardcoded priors — they adapt to the actual statistics of images rather than a designer's intuition.

Like NLP Transformers, ViT follows scaling laws: bigger models + more data + more compute = better performance, with predictable power-law relationships. This made it possible to plan model sizes and training budgets in advance.

ViT requires large-scale pretraining (10M+ images) to match CNNs. This was a significant barrier to adoption — most researchers don't have access to JFT-300M. Subsequent work (DeiT, DINOv2) addressed this with better training recipes and self-supervised pretraining.

The 16×16 patch size is fixed at model design time. This means ViT cannot naturally handle images of arbitrary resolution — larger images require more patches, which changes the sequence length and may exceed the model's context. Modern variants (Swin Transformer, NaViT) address this with hierarchical or native-resolution approaches.

The [CLS] token is great for classification but not for dense prediction (segmentation, detection). For these tasks, you need per-patch representations, and ViT's flat architecture doesn't naturally provide multi-scale features the way CNN hierarchies do.
heading_path: [CLS] Token Is Limited for Dense Tasks

excerpt: For high-resolution images (e.g., 1024×1024 for detection), the number of patches grows quadratically (1024/16 = 64, so 64×64 = 4096 patches). Attention is O(4096²) = 16M operations per layer — expensive. Swin Transformer and other hierarchical approaches address this.

"Training data-efficient image Transformers". Showed that ViT can match CNNs with ImageNet-1K-only pretraining, using a distilled [CLS] token and better training recipes. Made ViT practical for researchers without access to JFT-scale data.

"Shifted Window Transformer". Hierarchical architecture with shifted local windows. Provides multi-scale features (like CNNs) and scales to high-resolution images. Became the standard for dense prediction tasks.
Self-supervised ViT pretraining at scale. Produces general-purpose visual features that match or exceed supervised pretraining. Used as the visual encoder in many multimodal LLMs.
"Native Resolution ViT". Processes images at their native resolution (variable patch count) rather than resizing to fixed 224×224. More efficient and flexible.
Sigmoid loss for image-text pretraining (replaces softmax contrastive loss). Better than CLIP for many downstream tasks.
ViT reshaped computer vision:

1. **Transformers became the default for vision**. By 2022, most new vision models were Transformer-based. CNNs remain useful (especially for efficiency-constrained applications) but are no longer the research frontier.
2. **Cross-domain transfer of NLP innovations**. FlashAttention, RoPE, scaling laws — all developed for NLP — apply directly to vision Transformers. This synergy accelerated both fields.

3. **Foundation for multimodal models**. CLIP, Flamingo, BLIP, LLaVA, Gemini all use ViT-family encoders for the visual modality. ViT made multimodal models practical by providing a Transformer-compatible visual representation.

4. **Self-supervised visual representation**. ViT's architecture enabled DINO, DINOv2, MAE, and other self-supervised methods that learn visual features without labels. These features now power most production vision systems.

5. **End of architecture search**. Before ViT, vision researchers spent significant effort designing CNN architectures (ResNet, EfficientNet, RegNet). After ViT, the architecture question was largely settled — use a Transformer, focus on data and training. This freed research effort for other problems.

For AI engineers, ViT is the foundation of modern computer vision. If you're working with CLIP, LLaVA, SAM, or any vision-language model, you're using ViT-family encoders. Understanding ViT clarifies how images are processed and why certain design choices (patch size, [CLS] token, positional embeddings) matter.

> [!info] TL;DR
> Swin Transformer introduced **shifted-window attention** — attention is computed within local windows, and the windows are shifted between layers so that information flows across window boundaries. Combined with a hierarchical architecture (patch merging reduces resolution as depth increases), Swin provides multi-scale features like CNNs while maintaining Transformer expressivity. Swin became the standard for dense vision tasks (detection, segmentation) where ViT's fixed resolution and lack of hierarchy were limitations.
Liu, Z., Lin, Y., Cao, Y., Hu, H., Wei, Y., Zhang, Z., Lin, S., & Guo, B. (2021). *Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows*. ICCV 2021 (Best Paper). arXiv:2103.14030.
[[21 - Vision Transformer ViT 2020|ViT]] (2020) showed that Transformers work for vision, but it had two limitations for dense prediction tasks (object detection, semantic segmentation):

1. **Fixed resolution**: ViT processes images at a single resolution (e.g., 224×224 → 14×14 patches). Dense prediction tasks require multi-scale features — coarse features for global context, fine features for localization. ViT's flat architecture doesn't provide this.

2. **Global attention cost**: ViT computes attention over all patches, which is O(N²) in the number of patches. For high-resolution images (e.g., 800×1333 for COCO detection), this is prohibitively expensive.

CNNs solve both problems via hierarchical architectures (ResNet, FPN) that produce features at multiple resolutions. Swin Transformer brings this hierarchical structure to Transformers, with a key innovation that enables local attention to flow across windows.
Swin processes images in 4 stages, each reducing spatial resolution by 2× and doubling channel dimension:

The first stage splits the image into 4×4 patches and embeds them. Subsequent stages merge 2×2 neighboring patches (concatenate their features, project to 2× channels). This mirrors the downsampling in CNNs and provides multi-scale features for dense prediction.

Instead of computing attention over all patches, Swin computes attention within local windows. For a stage with H×W patches and window size M×M, the number of patches per window is M², and the number of windows is (H/M) × (W/M). Attention cost per layer: O((H/M) × (W/M) × M⁴) = O(H × W × M²), linear in image size.
The window size M is typically 7. This gives attention over 49 patches per window — much cheaper than attention over all 784 patches (28×28) in stage 2.
Window attention has a problem: patches in different windows cannot communicate. Information is confined to windows, and there's no cross-window flow.
Swin solves this by shifting the windows between layers:

- Layer `l`: windows are at positions `(0, 0), (0, M), (M, 0), (M, M), ...`
- Layer `l+1`: windows are shifted by `(M/2, M/2)`, so they straddle the previous window boundaries.
With shifting, a patch in window A (layer `l`) is in a window that includes patches from windows A, B, C, D (layer `l+1`). Information flows across original window boundaries.

```mermaid graph TD subgraph Layer l: Standard Windows A1[Window A
patches 0-48] B1[Window B
patches 49-97] C1[Window C
patches 98-146] D1[Window D
patches 147-195] end subgraph Layer l+1: Shifted Windows A2[Shifted window
patches from A, B, C, D] B2[Shifted window
patches from A, B, C, D] C2[Shifted window
patches from A, B, C, D] D2[Shifted window
patches from A, B, C, D] end Note[Alternating layers: standard then shifted
→ information flows across windows] ```

Naive implementation of shifted windows is inefficient (the shifted windows at the edges are partial). Swin uses a clever trick: cyclically shift the feature map so that the shifted windows align with standard windows, compute attention, then cyclically shift back. This avoids partial windows and makes the implementation efficient.

Swin adds a learned relative position bias to the attention scores: `Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d) + B) V`, where `B` is a learned bias that depends on the relative position of the query and key within the window. This is similar to [[16 - Transformer-XL 2019|Transformer-XL]]'s relative positional encoding but applied to 2D vision patches.

The relative position bias is parameterized as a small learnable table (size `(2M-1) × (2M-1)` for window size M). It captures 2D spatial relationships (e.g., "attend to the token above-right") that are important for vision but not for text.
Swin Transformer achieved SOTA on ImageNet classification, COCO object detection, and ADE20K semantic segmentation:

| Task                          | Previous SOTA    | Swin Transformer |
|-------------------------------|------------------|------------------|
| ImageNet-1K (top-1)           | 88.5 (ViT-Huge)  | 87.3 (Swin-L)    |
| COCO detection (AP^box)       | 55.1             | 58.7 (Swin-L)    |
| ADE20K segmentation (mIoU)    | 48.4             | 53.5 (Swin-L)    |

The most striking results were on dense prediction (detection and segmentation): Swin outperformed previous SOTA by 3.6 and 5.1 points respectively. This was the first Transformer to clearly beat CNN-based methods (DetectoRS, SETR) on dense prediction, validating the hierarchical approach.
On ImageNet classification, Swin slightly underperformed ViT-Huge (which had more pretraining data), but it was much more efficient (similar accuracy with fewer parameters and FLOPs).

Dense prediction tasks require multi-scale features. Swin's hierarchical architecture (4 stages, each with half the resolution) provides this naturally, matching the structure of CNN feature pyramids (FPN, PAN). ViT's flat architecture doesn't.

Without shifting, window attention is too local — each window is isolated, and the model cannot integrate information across the image. Shifting solves this elegantly: alternating layers with standard and shifted windows create cross-window connections while keeping attention local.
W-MSA is O(H × W × M²) — linear in image size. This makes Swin practical for high-resolution images (detection at 800×1333, segmentation at 512×2048), where ViT's O(H² W²) would be prohibitive.
The learned relative position bias captures 2D spatial relationships that are essential for vision. This generalizes better than absolute position embeddings, especially for variable image sizes.
The window size M is fixed at model design time. This means Swin cannot adaptively choose attention patterns based on content — the windows are the same regardless of what's in the image.

The hierarchical downsampling (patch merging) loses spatial detail. For tasks requiring fine-grained localization (small object detection, boundary-aware segmentation), this can hurt. Modern variants (Swin-V2, CSWin) address this with adaptive merging or different window patterns.

While linear in image size, Swin's constant factors are still significant. For very high-resolution images (e.g., 4K satellite imagery), even Swin is expensive. Techniques like sparse attention or hierarchical dilated windows extend further.

NaViT (2023) and other native-resolution ViTs process images at their original resolution without fixed patch sizes. For some tasks, this is simpler and more effective than Swin's hierarchical approach.
Improved scaling: larger window sizes, scaled cosine attention, log-spaced continuous position bias. Scaled to 3B parameters and achieved SOTA on more benchmarks.
Cross-shaped window attention: horizontal and vertical strips instead of square windows. Better global context with similar efficiency.
Self-supervised pretraining for ViT-family models, including Swin. Showed that Swin can be pretrained without labels and match supervised performance.
Self-supervised ViT pretraining at scale. Uses standard ViT (not Swin) but achieves SOTA on dense prediction, suggesting that with enough data, flat architectures can match hierarchical ones.
Swin Transformer's influence on computer vision:

1. **Standard for dense prediction**. Swin became the default backbone for object detection and semantic segmentation in 2022–2023. Most SOTA detection and segmentation models used Swin as the encoder.

2. **Hierarchical Transformers as a paradigm**. Swin showed that hierarchical architecture (multi-scale features) is valuable for Transformers, not just for CNNs. This influenced architectures in other domains (video, 3D, medical imaging).

3. **Shifted window as a technique**. The shifted-window idea (alternate local windows with shifted versions) appears in modified form in several subsequent architectures. The general principle — use local attention but ensure cross-window flow — became standard.

4. **Relative position bias for 2D**. Swin's relative position bias (a 2D learned table) influenced how vision Transformers handle position. Modern vision Transformers (NaViT, DINOv2) use RoPE-2D or similar relative encodings.

5. **Bridge to multimodal**. Swin's hierarchical features are used as visual encoders in some multimodal LLMs. The multi-scale features are particularly useful for tasks that require both global understanding and local detail (e.g., document understanding, chart reading).

For AI engineers working on vision tasks, Swin remains a strong choice for dense prediction. If you're doing object detection, semantic segmentation, or any task that benefits from multi-scale features, Swin (or its variants) is a standard option.

> [!info] TL;DR
> DeiT v2 (2024) revisits the original DeiT recipe (2020) in light of five years of vision-transformer advances. The paper shows that the simple DeiT recipe — strong data augmentation + teacher distillation + careful initialization — when updated with modern components (LayerScale, PatchDropout, ReLU², EMA teacher) and modern training recipes (longer training, larger datasets) closes most of the gap to Swin Transformer and ConvNeXt. DeiT v2 is the canonical reference for "how to train a vision transformer efficiently" in 2024–2026 and is widely used as the vision encoder backbone in vision-language models (LLaVA, etc.).

- **InternViT (2024)**: scales DeiT v2 to 6B parameters; used as InternVL's vision encoder.
- **NaViT (2024)**: variable-resolution ViT, breaks the fixed-resolution constraint; uses DeiT v2-style recipe.

excerpt:
- **Plain ViT vs hierarchical**: DeiT v2 confirms plain ViT is competitive, but for very high-resolution tasks (object detection at 1024×1024+), hierarchical features (Swin) may still be better. The trade-off is unresolved.
- **PatchDropout and receptive field**: aggressive PatchDropout (50%+) reduces the effective receptive field. Does this hurt tasks that require global structure (counting, spatial reasoning)? Early evidence is mixed.
- **EMA teacher vs CNN teacher**: DeiT v2's EMA teacher is simpler (no separate model needed) but may not provide as rich gradients as a CNN teacher (which has different inductive biases). The trade-off is not fully characterized.
- **Video extension**: DeiT v2 is image-only. Extending to video (with temporal attention) is an open problem.

1. **Q: What changed between DeiT (2021) and DeiT v2 (2024)?**
   A: Five main updates: (1) **LayerScale** (per-channel residual scaling) for deep-ViT stability. (2) **PatchDropout** (randomly drop patches) for efficiency and regularization. (3) **ReLU²** activation (vs GELU) — simpler kernels, same quality. (4) **EMA teacher** instead of a CNN teacher — no separate model needed. (5) **Longer training** (500 epochs vs 300) with **TrivialAugment** (vs RandAugment). The result: DeiT v2 matches or beats Swin/ConvNeXt at every scale, with fewer parameters and FLOPs.

2. **Q: Why is DeiT v2 used as the vision encoder in VLMs like LLaVA?**
   A: Three reasons. (1) **Simple structure**: plain ViT (no shifted windows, no hierarchical features, no convolutions) is easier to integrate with LLMs. (2) **Single-scale features**: Swin produces hierarchical features (multiple resolutions); plain ViT produces one feature map, which is what VLMs expect. (3) **Strong quality**: DeiT v2's ImageNet accuracy is competitive with Swin/ConvNeXt, so the vision encoder quality is sufficient. Most 2024–2026 VLMs (LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, InternVL, Qwen-VL) use DeiT-v2-style encoders.

3. **Q: When would you choose DeiT v2 vs DINOv2?**
   A: **DeiT v2** for supervised classification (when you have labels) — better ImageNet accuracy, simpler training. **DINOv2** for self-supervised pretraining (when you don't have labels) — better transfer learning, can be fine-tuned downstream. Most production VLMs use either: DeiT v2 for the supervised case, DINOv2 for the self-supervised case. SigLIP-2 (2025) combines both — self-supervised pretraining + supervised fine-tuning.
